company: Zerodha (founded by Nithin and Nikhil Kamath)
headline: HOW ZERODHA BUILT A PROFITABLE BROKERAGE WITHOUT VENTURE CAPITAL
post_text: A stock broker that has never taken venture money still reported a net profit of Rs 4,237 crore for FY25. Zerodha, started in 2010, is that broker, and its growth came from its own customers.
thread: A stock broker that has never taken venture money still reported a net profit of Rs 4,237 crore for FY25. Zerodha, started in 2010, is that broker, and its growth came from its own customers.

Zerodha is a discount stock broker run by brothers Nithin and Nikhil Kamath. It charges nothing for equity delivery trades and a flat fee on most other trades. Brokerage is its main income, with smaller amounts from other fees and interest.

Many brokers took a cut on every trade. Zerodha went the other way, using flat-fee pricing instead of high commissions. Its 2015 pricing set delivery trades at zero, and it grew without outside funding.
The model paid off in scale. Revenue reached Rs 9,994.5 crore in FY24, and Zerodha held a 15.8 per cent market share with 7.26 million users. FY25 revenue then fell 11.2 per cent as rules tightened.

company: Shri Mahila Griha Udyog Lijjat Papad
headline: HOW SEVEN MUMBAI WOMEN TURNED RS 80 INTO A PAPAD COOPERATIVE WORTH MILLIONS
post_text: Seven women in Mumbai started a papad business in 1959 with a sum of just Rs 80. Their cooperative now reports more than $200 million in sales.
thread: Seven women in Mumbai started a papad business in 1959 with a sum of just Rs 80. Their cooperative now reports more than $200 million in sales.
Lijjat makes papads, masalas, wheat flour, chapatis and detergent, and sells them in India and abroad. It is a cooperative, so each member is a co-owner and profits are shared equally.
Lijjat has no single owner. Women roll papad from home through local branches, and any woman who wants to join can approach one. The papad is kept to one standard, and quality is never compromised.
Open membership and fixed quality kept it growing. It employs more than 43,000 women, runs 82 branches across 17 states, and has never struggled to give work to new members.

company: Amul (Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation, GCMMF)
headline: HOW AMUL'S FARMER-POOLED CO-OP TURNED MILK INTO A RS 1 LAKH CRORE BRAND
post_text: A dairy brand built by 36 lakh farmers pushed its turnover past Rs 1 lakh crore in FY 2025-26. That was an 11% rise on a Rs 90,000 crore base the year before.
thread: A dairy brand built by 36 lakh farmers pushed its turnover past Rs 1 lakh crore in FY 2025-26. That was an 11% rise on a Rs 90,000 crore base the year before.

Amul runs as three layers. Village societies collect milk, district unions process and test it, and a state federation markets the finished products under the Amul name. It also makes dairy goods for other brands.
Rather than dealing with each farmer one by one, Amul groups small milk producers into village-level societies. Much of the money shoppers pay is sent back to those farmers.
That structure has paid off in numbers. Turnover reached Rs 1 lakh crore in FY 2025-26, and the International Cooperative Alliance has ranked Amul the world's No. 1 cooperative.

headline: HOW MEESHO GREW FROM A WHATSAPP SHOPPING IDEA INTO A LISTED E-COMMERCE COMPANY
post_text: Meesho, founded by Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Barnwal, raised $606 million in its IPO. On its first trading day, its shares rose as much as 46% above the issue price of Rs 111. (1/7)
thread: Meesho, founded by Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Barnwal, raised $606 million in its IPO. On its first trading day, its shares rose as much as 46% above the issue price of Rs 111. (1/7)

Founded in 2015, Meesho started as a WhatsApp-based social commerce app for first-time online shoppers. Its two founders, both IIT Delhi graduates, noticed small shopkeepers selling through WhatsApp groups. It is now Bengaluru-based. (2/7)

Meesho is an online marketplace where small sellers list products for buyers. Its sellers are mostly small merchants, and its buyers are value-conscious shoppers, many in Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns. (3/7)
Meesho mainly earns from logistics fees, advertising and other services, rather than taking a cut of every sale. Its separate Meesho Mall channel does charge commissions on products sold there. (4/7)

In its main marketplace, Meesho charges sellers little or no commission, which sets it apart from many rivals. Its asset-light setup and strong base in non-metro cities are central to its pitch. (5/7)

Losses were its biggest test. Its consolidated net loss was Rs 3,941.70 crore in FY25, and festive-season spending widened losses again to Rs 490.67 crore in the December 2025 quarter. It kept growing, and by the March 2026 quarter the loss had narrowed 88% to Rs 166 crore. (6/7)

In FY26, which ended March 2026, revenue rose about 35% to Rs 12,626 crore and net loss stood at Rs 1,358 crore. Lesson: fast growth with low prices still needs a clear route to profit, so track losses as closely as sales. (7/7)
story_text:
Meesho, founded by Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Barnwal, raised $606 million in its IPO. On its first trading day, its shares rose as much as 46% above the issue price of Rs 111.

Founded in 2015, Meesho started as a WhatsApp-based social commerce app for first-time online shoppers. Its two founders, both IIT Delhi graduates, noticed small shopkeepers selling through WhatsApp groups. It is now Bengaluru-based.

Meesho is an online marketplace where small sellers list products for buyers. Its sellers are mostly small merchants, and its buyers are value-conscious shoppers, many in Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns.

Meesho mainly earns from logistics fees, advertising and other services, rather than taking a cut of every sale. Its separate Meesho Mall channel does charge commissions on products sold there.

In its main marketplace, Meesho charges sellers little or no commission, which sets it apart from many rivals. Its asset-light setup and strong base in non-metro cities are central to its pitch.

Losses were its biggest test. Its consolidated net loss was Rs 3,941.70 crore in FY25, and festive-season spending widened losses again to Rs 490.67 crore in the December 2025 quarter. It kept growing, and by the March 2026 quarter the loss had narrowed 88% to Rs 166 crore.

In FY26, which ended March 2026, revenue rose about 35% to Rs 12,626 crore and net loss stood at Rs 1,358 crore. Lesson: fast growth with low prices still needs a clear route to profit, so track losses as closely as sales.

headline: HOW LENSKART BUILT A 3,624-STORE EYEWEAR CHAIN FROM AN ONLINE CONTACT LENS SHOP
post_text: Lenskart, founded by Peyush Bansal, Amit Chaudhary, Sumeet Kapahi and Neha Bansal, now runs 3,624 stores. That is more than Specsavers' 2,987, which places it near the top of global optical retail. (1/7)
thread: Lenskart, founded by Peyush Bansal, Amit Chaudhary, Sumeet Kapahi and Neha Bansal, now runs 3,624 stores. That is more than Specsavers' 2,987, which places it near the top of global optical retail. (1/7)

Lenskart began in Delhi, where the founders set up the company around 2008. It launched in November 2010 by selling contact lenses online. Peyush Bansal saw a market with little clutter and room for a new player. (2/7)

The company designs and makes most of its own eyeglasses, then sells them through its stores and app. Customers buy in India and abroad, and its eye tests rose 40.4% to 80 lakh in one recent quarter. (3/7)

Revenue comes mainly from selling eyewear. Memberships and services add to it: fee income was ₹73 crore in the latest quarter, and services revenue, including memberships and home eye check-ups, was ₹133 crore in FY25. (4/7)

Instead of routing glasses through several middlemen, Lenskart makes its own and keeps that margin. It also brings customers in through eye checks, first at home and later in clinics. Gross margin reached 70%. (5/7)

In FY17, losses of ₹262.87 crore were bigger than operating revenue of ₹179 crore. Bansal said the team kept pushing growth and refocused whenever the vision blurred. The first full-year profit came in FY20. (6/7)

Today it runs 3,624 stores, and net profit in the September 2026 quarter more than doubled to ₹227 crore. Its store growth was paid for from the business's own cash, a useful lesson for any founder: fund expansion from operations where you can. (7/7)
